newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST-US CPI seen up a moderate 0.3 pct in Oct.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-US CPI seen up a moderate 0.3 pct in Oct.

text.p: The Consumer Price Index (CPI) will rise in October, but not enough to suggest that U.S. inflation is in danger of breaking out of its subdued trend, economists said.
According to a Reuters survey, economists expect the CPI to increase by 0.3 percent in October, the same amount as in September.
Core CPI, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, is expected to increase 0.2 percent in October, compared to 0.3 percent in September, according to the survey.
"This will be the second staight month" that CPI increased by 0.3 percent, noted Ed McKelvey, senior economist at Goldman Sachs & Co Inc, "so it begins to look like inflation is picking up."
He also expects core CPI to increase by 0.3 percent.
But he argued, "This is not the beginning of something new. Much of the increase is to make up for earlier readings which were biased toward the downside."
McKelvey said October's CPI will reflect an increase in airline ticket prices after a tax increase on jet fuel.
Schaja predicts October CPI will increase by 0.3 percent while core CPI increases by 0.2 percent for the month.

"The increase in energy prices, which have come down recently, will bias this number upwards. If you look at the 0.2 percent core rate, this is a favorable report which suggests inflation at the consumer level is remaining contained."
Schaja added recent decreases in energy prices are likely to push CPI lower in November.

Cheryl Katz, senior economist at Merrill Lynch & Co, said the CPI growth coupled with continued moderate economic growth suggests there are few signs that inflation in the U.S. will pickup anytime soon.

"There are no bottleneck pressures in manufacturing and commodity prices are down. While wages are showing a yellow blinking (warning) light, the Employment Cost Index shows labor costs remain under control."
Katz expects CPI to increase by 0.2 percent in October and core CPI to increase by 0.1 percent during the same time.
"The biggest thing keeping prices low is global competitiveness. That shows no signs of abating," she added.
While the increase took place in September, it was not reflected in September's numbers, he said.

"With inflation giving a relatively tame performance alongside growth which has been slowing, I see no reason for the Federal Reserve to change its policy toward the tighter direction now. Down the road though, this will contribute to the appearance that inflation is picking up."

Marilyn Schaja, money market economist at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Securities Corp called a 0.3 percent CPI increase "significant," but says the increase is attributable primarily to higher energy prices in September and October.
